transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-03
Start time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Lisa Carter (Acme Eng Manager), Jason Wu (Acme Infra), Anita Patel (Acme SRE), Tom Reynolds (Acme Procurement)

-- Auto summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect) --
Redwood did a console walkthrough focused on tracing, error analysis, request logs; went over how to surface slow tokens, traceback to prompts, and how to attach request metadata for debugging. PoC and pricing next steps captured.

[00:00] Ethan (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, we really appreciate the time. I'm Ethan, I'm the account lead, and with me is Maya from our SE team who will drive the console demo.
[00:18] Maya (Redwood SE): Hi all, yeah great to meet you. Quick agenda: show tracing, request logs, error analysis, and then go through example debugging flows and how you'd use those in a PoC.
[00:30] Lisa (Acme): Thanks, we're excited. Main goals for us: understand root-cause for latency spikes, correlate errors to inputs and user sessions, and make sure we can meet data residency/compliance requirements.
[00:45] Jason (Acme): Also, we want to see how logs look because we have an existing ELK pipeline; we need to know how easy it is to export or stream logs.
[01:05] Maya: Totally. We'll show the Console first -- trace view and request logs -- then how to link traces to raw request payloads and token-level timing. There may be some transcribe issues on names, sorry if any product names come out weird.
[01:20] Ethan: Quick question, Lisa, do you know if the PoC will be Hosted or Dedicated? That influences how we show the private trace export options.
[01:30] Lisa: We're leaning Dedicated for predictable performance, but need to confirm with procurement. Tom is on the call, he'll chime in.
[01:40] Tom (Acme Procurement): Yes, we'll probably aim for Dedicated but need pricing and SLA. Also procurement wants to see SOC 2 and encryption at rest details.
[01:52] Ethan: Great, we'll include SOC 2 docs and KMS/HSM integration notes in the follow-up.
[02:05] Maya: Jumping in — opening Console now, apologies for any screen lag. So this is the Traces tab. Each row is a request trace; you can filter by model, route, status code, region, and custom tags like customer_id or session_id.
[02:25] [00:02:25] Maya: Here's a slow trace -- notice the waterfall shows token-level timings. The long pole is the attention kernel at step 3, and we can see the sequence length ballooned due to a long user prompt.
[02:40] Jason: That waterfall, is that computed from server-side telemetry or from client timestamps?
[02:48] Maya: Server-side; we collect per-step timing in the runtime and annotate the trace. There can be clock skew in distributed cases but we largely rely on server metrics.
[02:58] Anita (Acme): Can we attach our request IDs so the trace correlates to our logs?
[03:05] Maya: Yes, there's a custom tag field on the request that we ingest (x-acme-request-id), it becomes searchable and part of the trace metadata.
[03:18] Maya: Also, there's a 'View Request' button to open the raw prompt, headers, and the model config used (quantization profile, max tokens, top_p, etc).
[03:30] Lisa: That's helpful. How do you handle KV cache visibility? We often need to know if stale KV cache caused repetition or latency.
[03:40] Maya: We surface cache hits/misses per request as part of the trace; it's a summarized metric — 'KV hits: 24, misses: 2' — and you can expand to see prefixes that matched. Sometimes the naming in traces is a bit fuzzy, like 'KV cash' in older exports, but the data is there.
[03:58] Ethan: Side note — for Dedicated we can enable debug-level traces for a short window during the PoC to capture more detail, but that does increase retention and storage.
[04:15] Jason: What's the retention window and export options? We need to push to our ELK cluster.
[04:22] Maya: Default retention in Hosted is 30 days for traces; Dedicated can configure longer retention and you can stream to S3 or to your syslog/elk via our log-forwarder. We also support direct API pulls for request logs.
[04:38] Lisa: And encryption? Where are traces stored?
[04:42] Ethan: Traces are stored in the control plane for Hosted; Dedicated gives you an option to use a customer-managed VPC and S3 or a private object store. All data at rest is encrypted, KMS integration available. We'll attach the security whitepaper.
[04:58] Maya: Back to demo, here's the Error Analysis view. You can group by error type: timeout, model crash, rate-limited. The console also shows the stack snippet where the error originated, though sometimes the transcription of stack frames is coarse.
[05:15] [00:05:15] Maya: Example — we had a spike of timeouts from a particular route. Filtering by route + model version shows increased latencies and correlated memory pressure.
[05:28] Lisa: Can we set up alerts on that?
[05:31] Maya: Yes, you can create metric alerts on 95th percentile latency, error-rate, or custom tags. Alerts can route to PagerDuty, Slack, or email.
[05:42] Anita: For privacy/regulatory reasons we'd prefer logs without PII; is there a redaction layer?
[05:48] Maya: We have pipeline rules to redact or hash fields at ingestion; for Dedicated you can enforce redaction on the edge. We'll share examples of configs.
[06:00] Jason: Show us how to do a debugging flow — go from an error to identifying the root cause.
[06:06] Maya: Sure. Step one: find the failed trace. Step two: open raw request to see prompt. Step three: check token-level timing to see if latency is model compute vs network. Step four: cross-reference trace id with request-logs and infra metrics.
[06:24] [00:06:24] Maya: Here's a trace ID: trace_9a2b... I'm going to open request logs for that ID. You can see the headers include x-acme-session, and the prompt shows an unexpected system message repeating which inflated sequence length.
[06:40] Lisa: Interesting — that seems like our prompt concatenation microservice bug. So the root cause is upstream.
[06:46] Maya: Exactly, and with the trace you can see where the tokenization jump happened.
[06:50] Jason: On request logs, do you store full prompt text by default? We might want to disable that for PII reasons.
[06:57] Maya: By default we store the prompt and response for debugging, but you can configure to store hashes only, or redact specific fields. For PoC we can work with a sanitized data set.
[07:10] Ethan: Quick commercial note — that level of retention/redaction is typically part of the Dedicated contract addendum.
[07:18] Tom: Can you also explain rollbacks? If we deploy a new model and it regresses, how do we detect and rollback?
[07:26] Maya: Console has model version dashboards and quality regressions tied to eval sets. You can configure automatic fallback to a previous model if latency SLA breaches or quality drops beyond threshold.
[07:40] [00:07:40] Maya: Now I'll show the Request Logs tab — this is where raw events are stored. You can query by trace_id, request_id, session_id, or custom tags. Results show timestamp, status, latency_ms, and snippet of prompt/response.
[07:55] Anita: Can we export query results as JSON?
[07:58] Maya: Yep, export as ndjson or CSV, or stream results to an S3 bucket.
[08:05] Lisa: For our internal dashboards we prefer S3 and then ingest to Athena. That will work?
[08:10] Maya: Yes, S3 export + partitioning by date is standard and we provide an example Athena schema.
[08:20] Jason: What about sampling? If we have 100k requests per minute, we don't want to store everything.
[08:26] Maya: We support adaptive sampling and prefix caching so you can store all errors and a fraction of successes. For PoC we usually capture 100% of a small slice and sample the rest.
[08:38] [00:08:38] Maya: Demo pause — quick Q from Ethan: have you benchmarked expected 95p latency? What SLOs would you target?
[08:45] Lisa: Ideally 95th < 300ms for generation up to 512 tokens, but we can adjust depending on complexity.
[08:52] Maya: For that SLO I'd recommend Dedicated with optimized batching and a quantization profile we discussed earlier. We'll propose a config in the follow-up.
[09:05] Ethan: Also to note, our Optimize product can suggest batching settings per-route to hit cost/latency sweet spots.
[09:12] Jason: How intrusive are kernel/quantization changes in terms of output quality?
[09:17] Maya: There's a tradeoff; we run quality regressions on eval prompts and flag if output divergence exceeds X% by BLEU/ROUGE style or semantic evals. Typically int8/4-bit quantization is good but depends on model family.
[09:30] Lisa: Can the console show quality drift over time?
[09:33] Maya: Yes, you can tie eval suites to production routes and see regression alerts.
[09:40] [00:09:40] Maya: Back to tracing specifics — we also provide trace joining across microservices: if you propagate our trace_id through your services we can show end-to-end latency including your prompt construction time.
[09:55] Jason: We'll need that — our pipeline adds ~60ms occasionally.
[10:00] Maya: You can also upload your infra metrics to Console (prometheus metrics) and link them to traces for correlated graphs.
[10:10] Anita: On the PoC, can you run perf benchmarks in our region? We want to simulate our traffic pattern.
[10:16] Ethan: Yes, for Dedicated we can provision a benchmark harness that mirrors your qps and tokens-per-request. We'll schedule a run and share results.
[10:25] Lisa: We also need to check scaling — burst capacity and autoscaling behavior.
[10:30] Maya: Dedicated supports configured autoscaling policies and burst buffers; the console shows scaling events and model pool utilization in the Pools dashboard.
[10:40] [00:10:40] Maya: Quick demo of error aggregation — click 'Group by route' then 'Top errors' — you get a timeline and you can drill into a single error to see sample requests and the stack.
[10:55] Jason: Sample requests — are those raw? Again concerned about PII.
[10:58] Maya: They are raw but can be redacted; for this demo the sample is sanitized.
[11:05] Lisa: How do we connect the console to our SSO?
[11:09] Ethan: We support SAML/SSO, RBAC and SCIM for user provisioning. We'll send the SSO integration guide.
[11:18] Anita: For audit logs, can we get admin-level event retention longer?
[11:22] Maya: Yes, audit logs retention is configurable for Dedicated and can be shipped to your SIEM.
[11:30] [00:11:30] Maya: Now a short walkthrough of debugging flow with a real failure: showing a model crash due to OOM on a long prompt. The trace shows memory spikes, and we can see the model instance terminated; Console suggests enabling token-level batching reduction or switching to a model variant.
[11:50] Lisa: Would switching to a smaller model affect our output quality?
[11:54] Maya: Possibly; that's where Optimize comes in — it runs a quality/cost tradeoff and recommends model/quantization pairs and batching parameters.
[12:05] Ethan: There's also automatic fallback to a more robust model if the primary fails. That keeps user experience up.
[12:12] [00:12:12] Maya: Demo note: sometimes the auto-detected source of errors shows 'runtime.v3' or similar which isn't perfectly human readable; we can map those codes to clearer descriptions in your docs.
[12:25] Tom: A procurement question — if we do Dedicated with longer retention, what's the cost delta?
[12:30] Ethan: We'll include that in the pricing doc; generally retention and debug-level logging are tiered add-ons. We'll send a breakdown.
[12:40] Jason: On streaming responses, can traces show partial outputs timing?
[12:44] Maya: Yes, streaming token emission times are captured so you can see when the first byte was sent vs last token. Useful for UI jitter.
[12:55] Anita: For the trace sample rate, what's minimal to still be useful?
[12:59] Maya: For errors you want 100%; for successes you can sample 0.1-1% and still detect regressions depending on volume.
[13:10] [00:13:10] Maya: Quick pause — any blockers so far?
[13:15] Lisa: Only that we'd need to confirm procurement and security signoffs.
[13:20] Ethan: Understood — we'll follow up with SOC 2, encryption, and redaction configs.
[13:28] Maya: Now quick look at request-log query language — it's SQL-ish for filtering, or you can use UI filters. For advanced users we support regex and JSON path extraction.
[13:40] Jason: Great, we can pipe that into our alerting.
[13:44] [00:13:44] Maya: Also, we include a request replay feature in a sandbox mode — you can replay a request to a dev model instance for debugging without touching prod.
[13:55] Lisa: That sounds very helpful. Is the replay available for PII redacted requests?
[13:59] Maya: Yes, you can replay sanitized requests. The replay environment is isolated and doesn't count against prod quotas.
[14:10] Anita: For the PoC we'll need a list of required telemetry we need to forward — can you provide that?
[14:15] Maya: Yes — we'll send a telemetry checklist: trace_id propagation, request_id, session_id, user_id (optional/hash), model tags, route name, region, latency_ms, status, and raw prompt (optional).
[14:28] Ethan: I'll include that in the follow-up packet with the pricing.
[14:34] [00:14:34] Maya: Quick demo of triage: filter errors, pick earliest sample, open request, open call stack — then add a note and assign to an engineer. The note shows up in the console audit trail.
[14:46] Jason: That's good for cross-team handoffs.
[14:50] Lisa: Any gotchas for on-prem or VPC installs?
[14:54] Maya: On-prem has slightly different export tooling; you run the forwarder in your network. Also some kernel optimizations require GPUs with certain compute capability; our onboarding doc lists supported hardware.
[15:08] Anita: Could you attach that hardware compatibility matrix?
[15:11] Ethan: We'll include it.
[15:15] [00:15:15] Maya: Back to traces — there's also a 'compare traces' feature where you can overlay two traces to see divergence between model versions or configurations.
[15:28] Lisa: That could help when we A/B test.
[15:32] Maya: Exactly. You can run canary rollouts from the console and automatically compare quality/latency.
[15:40] [00:15:40] Maya: Quick note — in older exports some text labels came back munged, e.g., 'redwood console' spelled 'red wood' in transcription; ignore those minor name formatting issues.
[15:52] Ethan: We're going to share a deck and a short recorded clip of the tracing flow as well.
[15:58] Lisa: Nice. Regarding benchmarks, can you run a test that mimics our bursty traffic (spikes around 11am)?
[16:05] Ethan: Yes, we'll model the traffic pattern in the PoC harness.
[16:10] Jason: Will the PoC include latency p95/p99 reporting and model cost per 1M tokens?
[16:16] Maya: Yes, we'll provide cost and latency breakdowns per model and per route.
[16:22] [00:16:22] Maya: Now a quick look at tracing internals — we annotate each span with: step_name, duration_ms, token_count, hardware_id, and kernel name when available.
[16:33] Jason: Kernel name? Is that exposed to customers?
[16:36] Maya: We expose it in Dedicated and in the trace when debug-level logging enabled. It helps correlate performance anomalies to a specific kernel or compile path.
[16:48] Anita: That's useful.
[16:50] [00:16:50] Maya: Some caveats — sometimes model families use opaque kernel labels like 'attn_v2_opt'; we'll help map those in docs.
[16:58] Lisa: About export formats — do you support OpenTelemetry?
[17:02] Maya: We support OTLP for spans and metrics; you can send traces to your OTLP collector or we can ingest.
[17:10] Tom: Procurement question — for contract terms do you offer any uptime SLA credits?
[17:14] Ethan: For Dedicated we offer SLA backed credits; specifics are in the contract.
[17:20] [00:17:20] Maya: Demo: now showing request-log query with a join to infra metrics; here you can see CPU and GPU utilization correlated to a latency spike.
[17:33] Jason: Nice, that would help pinpoint infra vs model issues.
[17:37] Maya: Also, Console supports tagging requests during ingestion so if your frontend attaches 'experiment=search-v2' you can filter by that.
[17:46] Lisa: We run experiments frequently, so that will help.
[17:51] [00:17:51] Maya: Last feature highlight — you can create saved queries and dashboards and share them with stakeholders.
[17:58] Lisa: Can dashboards be embedded in internal Confluence?
[18:01] Maya: Yes, via an embed link with access controls.
[18:07] [00:18:07] Ethan: Alright, wrapping up the demo portion. Any further technical deep-dive requests?
[18:13] Jason: We might want a SE session on kernel tuning and quantization impact on quality.
[18:18] Maya: Happy to run that in a follow-up technical deep dive.
[18:22] Anita: And SRE will need a session on log-forwarder and retention config.
[18:26] Ethan: We'll set both.
[18:30] [00:18:30] Lisa: For timelines — if we kick off PoC week of 9/8 how long before we have benchmark results?
[18:36] Maya: Typical PoC runs for 2 weeks with a benchmark in the first week and tuning in the second; we'll deliver a report at the end.
[18:45] Tom: Procurement needs an initial quote to start approvals.
[18:48] Ethan: We'll send a ballpark and a dedicated pricing sheet.
[18:52] [00:18:52] Maya: Any last questions?
[18:55] Lisa: One more — how do you instrument client-side latency vs server-side?
[18:59] Maya: We recommend passing client timestamps in headers; we ingest them and compute client-server delta but it's best-effort.
[19:08] Jason: If timestamps are unreliable due to clock skew, how do you correct?
[19:12] Maya: We do some heuristics and you can enable NTP sync or instrument a health check. For critical flows we use server-side measurements as primary.
[19:25] [00:19:25] Ethan: Okay we'll capture all follow-ups — to recap we'll send pricing, SOC 2 and KMS docs, telemetry checklist, and schedule PoC + two technical deep dives.
[19:38] Lisa: Sounds good. Thank you both.
[19:42] Tom: Thanks.
[19:45] Anita: Thanks.
[19:46] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up by Friday with docs and calendar invites.
[19:52] Ethan: Bye all.
[44:30] End of recording (approx)
